cases.user_message: Здравствуйте. Я работаю senior-разработчиком в компании в Остине (Техас), при приёме в 2023 году подписал non-compete: 18 месяцев не работать на конкурентов по всей территории США. Сейчас мне предложили оффер в конкурирующем стартапе. Коллега сказал, что FTC ещё в 2024 году запретила все неконкуренции по всей стране, и мой договор в этой части ничего не стоит, можно спокойно уходить. Это так? Могу я просто подписать оффер и не переживать?
cases.why_in_scope: The skill states that the FTC non-compete rule is dead (vacated in court, and the FTC dropped its appeals on 2025-09-05), that non-competes are heavily state-driven, and that US law must not be treated as monolithic. A strong model with older knowledge may say the rule is merely stayed or pending appeal, or may accept the colleague's claim that non-competes were banned nationwide, instead of sending the user to Texas state law.
rubric: Says the FTC's nationwide non-compete ban never took effect: it was set aside by a federal court and the FTC later abandoned its appeals, so it does not void the user's agreement

Explains that enforceability is governed by state law (here Texas), where non-competes can be enforced if reasonable in time, geography and scope of activity, and that a court may narrow an overbroad restriction rather than simply void it

Gives practical next steps grounded in the facts: review the agreement's actual terms and choice-of-law clause, assess whether the nationwide 18-month scope is likely overbroad, and get a Texas employment attorney to review before signing the offer
Includes a disclaimer that this is informational and not legal advice and that a licensed attorney in the relevant state should be consulted

cases.user_message: We're a 40-person SaaS company, Delaware C-corp, HQ in Denver. We need to let one of our customer success reps go next Friday. Performance has been mediocre for a while, but honestly nothing is documented: no PIP, no written warnings. He's been with us a bit over two years, fully remote the whole time (he lives up in Bozeman). Our handbook has a clear at-will clause and he signed the acknowledgment when he started. Plan is a short call, no reason given, two weeks severance. Can you give me a quick checklist of what HR should have ready before Friday so we're covered legally?
cases.why_in_scope: The skill says at-will employment is the default in 49 states with Montana as the exception, and warns against treating US law as monolithic: identify the state whose law applies. The user never questions at-will status and mentions Bozeman only in passing, framing the request as a routine termination checklist; a strong model may write a generic at-will checklist (or focus on Colorado/Delaware) and miss that Montana's Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act requires good cause after the probationary period.
rubric: Flags that the employee works in Montana, the one state that is not at-will: after the probationary period, its Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act requires good cause for discharge, so the signed at-will acknowledgment does not settle the matter
Identifies that the employee's work location (Montana) rather than Delaware incorporation or the Denver HQ is what likely determines the governing employment law

Adapts the plan to the good-cause problem with concrete steps before Friday, such as documenting legitimate performance-based reasons (or reconsidering the timing/no-reason approach), checking any written probation and grievance policies, offering the severance in exchange for a signed release, and having a Montana employment lawyer review
Includes a disclaimer that this is informational and not legal advice, and recommends consulting an attorney admitted in the relevant state

checker_notes: Case 2 was too leading (it asserted 'everyone in the US is at-will' next to 'Bozeman, Montana'), so I rewrote it as a routine termination-checklist request with Bozeman mentioned only in passing, and tightened rubric items 1 and 3 to match.
